insider_note: With a constant term in both the numerator and the denominator, three unknowns A, B, C are needed instead of two — the third equation comes from matching the constant terms on both sides, not from a trig coefficient.

steps.label: Write the numerator as A·Dr + B·Dr′ + C and solve for A, B, C
lines: The numerator carries a constant as well, so

lines.text: it needs three parts: A times the

lines: Compare the coefficients on both sides:
Coeff of sinx: 3A−4B=2, coeff of cosx:
steps.why: A constant term in the denominator needs a THIRD free constant C. A·Dr does produce a constant, 5A, but A is already fixed by the sinx and cosx equations (A = 18/25, so 5A = 18/5), and 18/5 is not the 4 the numerator needs — C makes up the difference.
common_mistakes: Using only two unknowns A, B and forgetting C, which cannot balance the constant term 4 on the left.
Matching the constant equation as 5A=4 instead of 5A+C=4.
steps.memory_tip: Constant term present in Dr ⇒ a third unknown C is needed, matched from the constant-term equation alone.

steps.label: Substitute back and split the integral into three parts

lines.text: The first gives x, the second log|Dr|:

steps.why: Three unknowns give three separate pieces: A pairs with the denominator itself (a plain x term), B pairs with the denominator's derivative (a log term), and C is left multiplying a genuine ∫dx/Dr that still needs its own substitution.
common_mistakes: Trying to integrate C∫dx/Dr the same way as the log term — it is NOT an f′/f form and needs the tan(x/2) substitution instead.
Mixing up which coefficient (A or B) belongs with which piece.
steps.memory_tip: A goes with plain x, B goes with the log, C is the leftover piece that still needs its own substitution.

steps.label: Reduce the remaining integral by the tan(x/2) substitution
steps.why: This particular denominator happens to be a PERFECT square in t, (t+3)², which turns the leftover integral into a simple power-rule antiderivative rather than another log or Tan⁻¹.
common_mistakes: Not spotting that t²+6t+9 factors as a perfect square, and instead trying to complete the square as a sum or difference.
Believing that d/dt[−1/(t+3)] = −1/(t+3)². It is actually +1/(t+3)², which is exactly why ∫2dt/(t+3)² comes out as −2/(t+3)+c and not +2/(t+3)+c.
steps.memory_tip: t²+6t+9 = (t+3)² exactly — recognise the perfect square before reaching for the log or Tan⁻¹ formula.

steps.label: Combine for the final answer
steps.why: Multiplying C = 2/5 by the −2/(t+3) just found gives −4/(5(t+3)), and writing t back as tan(x/2) completes the three-term answer in the original variable x.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to multiply C=2/5 into the −2/(t+3) result before adding it to the other two terms.
Leaving the final term in terms of t instead of tan(x/2).
steps.memory_tip: (2/5)×(−2/(t+3)) = −4/(5(t+3)) — carry C through the substitution's result, don't just tack it on unmultiplied.
